title: Ask, Don't Argue
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Andrea Chiarelli makes the case for question-based persuasion over argument-based persuasion, drawing on a range of sources including Daryl Davis's decades-long practice of befriending KKK members, Oren Klaff's investment negotiation framework, and Haidt's moral foundations theory. The core argument is that direct argumentation triggers psychological reactance — the defensive posture that makes people more committed to their positions — while questions invite self-examination in ways that argumentation cannot. Chiarelli presents specific techniques: steel-manning the opponent's position before presenting your own, addressing feelings before facts (the 99%/1% formula from negotiation), using 'What would stop us?' rather than 'Why should we?', and going for a 'no' response rather than 'yes' to reduce defensiveness. The article is practical and technique-focused, grounded in research on how persuasion actually works.
points: Direct argumentation triggers psychological reactance — the hardening of position under felt pressure — while questions invite voluntary self-examination, which is the only route to genuine position change.

Daryl Davis spent decades persuading KKK members to leave by befriending them and asking questions, not by arguing. He has personally collected over 200 robes. His method is the empirical demonstration of this principle.

Steel-manning — presenting the strongest version of the opposing argument before your own — is not courtesy. It is a persuasion technique: it demonstrates that you have genuinely understood the other position, which is the pre-condition for them to consider yours.

The 99%/1% formula from negotiation: spend 99% of your persuasion effort addressing the emotional reality of the situation, and 1% on the logical case. Emotions are the real decision drivers even when logic is the stated one.
Going for 'no' rather than 'yes' reduces the defensiveness that drives rejection: when someone says 'no' they feel in control, which paradoxically makes them more open to reconsidering.
quotes: Daryl Davis did not argue people out of the Klan. He befriended them and asked questions. He has 200 robes. The argument-makers do not have 200 robes.
When you argue, you give people a position to defend. When you ask, you give them a problem to think about. Those are different cognitive states with very different outcomes.
Steel-manning is not about being fair. It is about being effective. You cannot persuade someone who believes you have not understood them.
The 99% of a persuasion conversation is emotional. The logic is the 1% you reach for once the emotional ground has been cleared. Most persuaders spend their time in the wrong 1%.
